name: Device Bound Session Credentials
plain: A device held key that stops stolen session cookies from working on another computer.
meaning: The site gets short lived cookies refreshed with a signature from a key kept in the TPM or secure hardware. Reveals that the session is tied to one device. Chrome 146 on Windows (Apr 2026); GA for Google Workspace on May 25 2026.

web.api: Secure-Session-Registration and Secure-Session-Response headers; bound session cookie

access.persistence: Cookie lifetime in minutes, refreshed by key proof until session ends
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can tie your sign in to this device so copied cookies stop working elsewhere
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you sign in on a site that uses it.
can: Create a key that stays on your device when you sign in
Check regularly that the session comes from your device
Refresh short lived cookies, while your device keeps proving itself
Cut off a session copied to another computer
cannot: Stop someone using your device while you are signed in
Move the key to another device
limits.reach_label: Your device and your sign in
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge on computers only. Firefox, Safari and phones do not support it.

story.what_it_is: A device held key that stops stolen login cookies from working on another computer.

marketing.name: Device Bound Session Credentials
marketing.pitch: Chrome pitches it as protection that ties a login session to your device, so stolen cookies are useless.

story.for_you: You see nothing. In the background your device proves it is the same one that signed in. If malware steals your cookie, it will not work elsewhere.
story.for_makers: It fights account takeover by cookie theft, a growing problem for banks, email and work tools. Makers keep users safer with no extra steps. It also ties a session to a specific device.

use_cases.example: Malware steals your email session cookie, but the attacker cannot use it on their own computer.
A bank keeps your session tied to your laptop so a stolen cookie cannot move money.
A social site stops account takeovers where hackers reuse stolen sessions.
A company ties staff sessions to company laptops so stolen sessions are useless.
A game store account protects your items and wallet from hijacked sessions.
A payment site keeps the session tied to your device to block fraud.
An ad account dashboard stays safe, since stolen sessions are a common way to hijack ad budgets.

technical_bounds: Needs hardware key support (TPM on Windows)
Chrome only so far, macOS later (verify version)
Short lived cookie must refresh often
